A B S T R A C T
Background
All newborns admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) experience pain during routine care and are at increased risk of long-
term adverse efects.
Endotracheal suctioning (ETS) is one of the most frequently performed procedures in the NICU, causing moderate-to-severe pain.
Approximately 50% of extremely preterm neonates require intubation and repeated ETS.
Objectives
To evaluate the benefits and harms of pharmacological interventions for the prevention of pain during ETS in mechanically ventilated
neonates.
Search methods
We searched Cochrane CRS, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL and three trial registries, together with reference checking. The latest search date
was August 2024.
Selection criteria
We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-, cluster- and cross-over RCTs of neonates (term and preterm) who were
mechanically ventilated via endotracheal or tracheostomy tube and required ETS. Pharmacological interventions were compared to
placebo, no intervention, or standard care, or to non-pharmacological interventions.
Data collection and analysis
Critical outcome measures were validated by composite pain scores. Secondary outcomes included physiological and behavioural pain
indicators.
We used standard Cochrane methods. For continuous outcomes, we used a fixed-efect model and reported mean diferences (MDs) with
95% confidence intervals (CIs). For categorical outcomes, we reported the typical risk ratio (RR) and risk diference (RD) and 95% CIs. We
assessed the certainty of the evidence using GRADE.

Main results
We included seven RCTs (1242 participants); six included preterm neonates; one included term neonates; four were included in a meta-
analysis.
Opioids (morphine, alfentanil, meperidine) versus placebo (four studies)
The evidence is very uncertain for the following outcomes (all very low-certainty): morphine may have little to no efect on Premature
Infant Pain Profile (PIPP) (MD -0.11; 95% CI -0.28 to 0.06; I2 = 93%; 4 studies, 1123 participants). The use of 20 µg/kg of alfentanil may reduce
the pain score (CHEOPS) change from baseline (median = not specified (NS); IQR = NS; P = 0.031; 1 study; 10 participants). Results afer 10
µg/kg of alfentanil were not reported. The use of 20 µg/kg of alfentanil may reduce heart rate change from baseline (median = NS; IQR =
NS; P = 0.031; 1 study; 10 participants). Results afer 10 µg/kg were not specified. Morphine may have little to no efect on the duration of
mechanical ventilation (MD -4.70; 95% CI -11.07 to 1.67; I2 = not applicable (NA); 1 study, 45 participants).
Meperidine may reduce behavioural pain score (BPS) (MD -2.7; P = 0.001; 1 study, 84 participants; low-certainty). Morphine may not increase
the risk of arterial hypotension (RR 1.49; 95% CI 95% 0.88 to 2.51; I2 = 57%; 2 studies, 928 participants; low-certainty).
Morphine probably does not reduce the incidence of severe intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH) (RR 1.13; 95% CI 0.80 to 1.61; I2 = 36%; I2
= 36%; 4 studies, 1065 participants; moderate-certainty).
No studies reported adverse events (AE) associated with morphine and meperidine; severe muscle rigidity was observed with alfentanil.
Opioids (morphine) versus sedatives (midazolam) (one study)
The evidence is very uncertain for the following outcomes (all very low-certainty): morphine may have little to no efect on PIPP score (MD
-1.00; 95% CI -2.66 to 0.66; I2 = NA; 1 study, 46 participants); CHEOPS not reported. Morphine may result in a large reduction in the duration
of mechanical ventilation (MD -6.70; 95% CI -12.40 to -1.00; I2 = NA; 1 study, 46 participants).
Morphine may not reduce the incidence of severe IVH (RR 0.08; 95% CI 0.00 to 1.43; 1 study, 46 participants; low-certainty).
No studies reported on physiological and behavioural indicators or haemodynamic changes.
No AEs were reported.
Sedatives (ketamine, midazolam) versus placebo (two studies)
Midazolam may reduce PIPP scores (MD -3.80; 95% CI -5.89 to -1.71; I2 = NA; 1 study, 45 participants; low-certainty).
The evidence is very uncertain for the following outcomes (all very low-certainty). Ketamine 0.5 mg/kg and 2 mg/kg may have little to no
efect on CHEOPS change from baseline (P = NS; 1 study, 16 participants). Ketamine 1 mg/kg may reduce CHEOPS change from baseline
(P = 0.043; 1 study, 16 participants). Ketamine 0.5 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg may have little to no efect on heart rate change from baseline (P =
NS; 1 study, 16 participants). Ketamine 2 mg/kg may increase heart rate change from baseline (P = 0.029; 1 study, 16 infants). The use of
0.5 mg/kg, 1 mg/kg and 2 mg/kg ketamine may have little to no efect on mean arterial blood pressure change from baseline (P = NS; 1
study, 16 participants; very low-certainty). Midazolam may have little to no efect on the duration of mechanical ventilation (MD 2.00; 95%
CI -5.14 to 9.14; I2 = NA; 1 study, 43 participants), and may have little to no efect on the risk of severe grade IVH (RR 1.59; 95% CI 0.43 to
5.84; I2 = NA; 1 study, 43 participants).
No studies reported behavioural indicators.
No AEs reported.
RoB assessment
Four studies had low RoB; three had high RoB: one for reporting bias; two for risk of carry-over efects.
Authors' conclusions
Morphine may have little to no efect on PIPP or duration of ventilation (evidence very uncertain). Morphine may not increase the risk of
hypotension and probably does not reduce the incidence of severe IVH. Alfentanil may reduce CHEOPS and heart rate change from baseline
(evidence very uncertain). Meperidine may reduce BPS.
Compared to midazolam, morphine may have little to no efect on PIPP scores, and may result in a large reduction in the duration
of ventilation (evidence very uncertain). No studies reported on physiological and behavioural indicators or haemodynamic changes.
Morphine may not reduce the incidence of severe IVH, compared to midazolam (low-certainty evidence).

P L A I N   L A N G U A G E   S U M M A R Y
Which medicines help reduce neonates' pain during lung suctioning?
Key messages:
We did not find enough good-quality evidence about the best medicines to treat pain during endotracheal suctioning.
Overall, it is unclear if the medications studied in this review reduce negative efects (harms) such as blood pressure and heart rate changes,
severe brain bleeding, or the length of time babies are on mechanical ventilators.
Larger, well-designed studies are needed to give better estimates of the benefits and potential harms of the diferent medications to treat
pain during endotracheal suctioning.
What is endotracheal (lung) suctioning?
Many neonates (newborn babies) have dificulty breathing. To help them, a mechanical ventilator (breathing apparatus) is used. The
ventilator works by inserting a flexible tube through the baby’s mouth or nose and down the windpipe (the trachea). The placement of the
tube is known as an endotracheal procedure (meaning access is obtained via the trachea). While the baby is attached to the ventilator, the
tube must be kept clean and clear. This process is called endotracheal suctioning.
What did we want to find out?
We wanted to find out how to reduce neonates' pain during endotracheal suctioning using pain-relieving or relaxing medications.
What did we do?
We searched medical databases for studies comparing two types of medicines to reduce neonates' pain during endotracheal suctioning.
Medicines included opioid painkillers such as morphine and alfentanil; sedatives (relaxing medications) such as midazolam; and
anaesthetics (medicines that slow down the brain and nervous systems' reactions to pain) such as ketamine.
What did we find?
We found seven studies of 1242 neonates. All studies took place in high-income countries. The largest study included 898 babies; the
smallest included 10; one study included 150 babies, and the remaining four included fewer than 100 babies. No studies were supported
financially by pharmaceutical companies.
Main results:
Outcomes during endotracheal suctioning
Opioids compared to placebo (a substance without medical efects)
It is unclear if morphine reduces pain or the length of time babies are on mechanical ventilation.
It is unclear if alfentanil reduces pain or heart rate.
Meperidine may reduce behavioural signs of pain such as crying.
Morphine may not cause low blood pressure.
Morphine probably reduces slightly the occurrence of severe brain bleeding.
Opioids compared to sedatives (midazolam)
It is unclear if morphine reduces pain.
Morphine may cause a large reduction in the length of time babies are on mechanical ventilation.
Morphine may not reduce the occurrence of severe cerebral haemorrhage (brain bleeding).
No studies reported blood pressure or heart rate changes, or behavioural signs of pain (such as crying).

What are the limitations of the evidence?
Confidence in our findings for our critical outcomes is low to very low because most studies were small, and there were too few studies
to be certain about the results.
Opioids vs placebo:
We are not confident that opioids (morphine, alfentanil) reduce pain or change heart rate.
We have little confidence that opioids (meperidine) reduce behavioural signs of pain.
Opioids vs sedatives:
We are not confident that opioids (morphine) reduce pain.
Sedatives vs placebo:
We are not confident that ketamine reduces pain or afects heart rate; behavioural signs of pain were not measured.
We have little confidence that midazolam reduces pain.
How up to date is this evidence?
The evidence is up-to-date until August 2024.

B A C K G R O U N D
Description of the condition
All newborns admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit
experience pain during routine care and are at increased risk of
long-term adverse efects (Campbell-Yeo 2022). Neonates are more
sensitive to nociceptive stimuli than older children; this is because
the functional ascending pain pathways capable of transmitting
noxious impulses are present by 24 weeks' gestation, whilst the
neurotransmitters modulating the ascending impulse are absent
until approximately 48 weeks' gestation (Anand 2000a; Hatfield
2014). Neuronal and synaptic organisation may be permanently
altered by repetitive painful experiences in term and preterm
neonates. The cerebral cortex is afected by multiple mechanisms
of neonatal pain and stress. Pain causes neuronal cell death,
and indirectly causes changes to the set-point of stress-sensitive
endocrine systems. Pain, when treated inadequately, results in
the immature pain system predisposing neonates to greater
clinical and behavioural sequelae (Anand 2000a). Both animal
experiments and human studies have shown that the immature
nervous system is highly responsive to tactile and noxious stimuli.
Neurophysiological recordings of newborn neonates undergoing
skin-breaking procedures reveal strong spinal nociceptive reflex
activity and distinct nociceptive cortical potentials in response to
these procedures (Cornelissen 2013; Fabrizi 2011; Slater 2010). The
younger the postnatal age of the infant, the more prolonged this
noxious evoked activity is (Fitzgerald 1984; Hatfield 2014).
With advances in perinatal services and neonatal intensive care
technology, the survival of extremely premature and compromised
neonates has increased substantially (Glass 2015). However,
despite medical advances, a considerable number of these
neonates have long-term sequelae, such as cerebral palsy,
neurosensory impairments, learning disabilities and respiratory
diseases (Glass 2015; Younge 2017). Newborn neonates admitted
to neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) are repeatedly and
persistently exposed to noxious stimuli, which results in profound
and long-lasting changes in nociceptive neural pathways (Slater
2010). For preterm neonates, this happens during a critical window,
towards the end of human gestation, where the relatively mature
foetus undergoes an important period of brain development,
peak rates of brain growth, exuberant synaptogenesis and the
developmental regulation of specific receptor populations (Anand
2000b; Bhutta 2002; Brummelte 2012).
Both term and preterm neonates may require endotracheal
intubation in the NICU. The most common causes are inadequate
respiratory drive (e.g. prematurity, apnoeas, perinatal asphyxia,
sepsis, neuromuscular disorders), obstructed airway (e.g. airway
malacia), and compromised pulmonary function (e.g. surfactant
deficiency, pneumonia, diaphragmatic hernia, pneumothorax)
(AAP 2021; Stein 2023).
To limit damage from ventilator-associated lung injury and
pneumonia, respiratory support in extremely preterm neonates
has shifed from primary mechanical ventilation to non-invasive
ventilation. However, approximately 50% of extremely preterm
neonates, born between 25 and 28 weeks, require intubation due
to severe respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) and poor respiratory
control. Below this age range, intubation rates progressively
increase with immaturity (Schulzke 2022).
When neonates are intubated, they require endotracheal
suctioning (ETS). This is a common procedure performed
worldwide on a daily basis (Schults 2021). Endotracheal suctioning
causes mild-to-moderate pain (Luo 2023). Even with improved
nursing performance and non-pharmacological interventions
during endotracheal suctioning, it remains associated with mild
pain (Hadian 2013; Pirlotte 2024).
Pain remains insuficiently recognised and ofen under-treated in
the NICU (Manworren 2016; Walker 2014). Neonates are dependent
on others to assess pain. Although objective and reliable pain
assessment is the basis for safe and adequate pain management,
there are still no fully objective pain assessment tools available
for this vulnerable population (Eriksson M 2019; Maxwell 2019).
Despite the large number of pain assessment tools available, we
still do not have a gold standard regarding the applicability of
these scales in a preverbal population with diferent pathologies.
The use of scales that have been validated for construct validity,
internal consistency, and inter-rater reliability is recommended.
Furthermore, it is recommended to choose a particular scale based
on the population and pathology of interest (Giordano 2019).
Description of the intervention
The neurodevelopmental outcomes of neonates may be afected
by pain. The most obvious and efective strategy to reduce pain
from repeated endotracheal suctioning is to reduce the frequency
of suctioning. In addition, many diferent non-pharmacological
interventions aimed at reducing stress during painful procedures
have been described and studied (Attarian 2014; Pillai Riddell 2023;
Pirlotte 2024).
Management of neonatal pain ofen includes opioid therapy.
Morphine and fentanyl are the most commonly used opioids in
the NICU (Attarian 2014). Paracetamol is the most commonly
prescribed analgesic for the treatment of acute pain in adults and
children and is a widely accepted treatment for moderate pain in
neonates (Meek 2012; Ohlsson 2020).
Pharmacological interventions are efective during a wide range
of acute procedures, but are not always accessible for procedures
that require frequent use. Endotracheal suctioning is performed an
average of seven times per day and is ofen administered by one
nurse or a respiratory therapist (Gardner 2009; Schults 2021).
How the intervention might work
Pharmacological interventions are commonly used for procedural
pain, but their usage is not evidence-based (Lago 2009). Analgesics
could reduce the transmission of noxious stimuli, reducing
observed behavioural distress and signs of physiological instability
(Moultrie 2017).
A summary of how these interventions might work is outlined
below.
1. Non-opioid analgesia: acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-
inflammatory drug agents. Because the mechanism of action
includes inhibition of prostaglandin formation, these drugs have
limited adverse efects with regard to respiratory depression.
They are used as adjuncts to opioid analgesia for moderate-to-
severe pain (Bhalla 2014).
a. Paracetamol: paracetamol is defined by the National Library
of Medicine as "a derivative of acetanilide with analgesic,

before the intervention, in reducing the efects of painful
procedures in neonates (Ohlsson 2020; Walker 2014).
b. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs): these drugs
have the ability to inhibit cyclooxygenase. There are limited
studies investigating the analgesic efect of NSAIDs on
neonates. Intravenously administered NSAIDs can be used
for analgesia in neonates when dosing is based on gestational
age. However, the purpose is to reduce opioid exposure.
Adverse efects, such as alterations in cerebral blood
flow, intraventricular haemorrhage, platelet dysfunction and
decreased Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) are described
in this population (Bhalla 2014). The use of NSAIDs for
procedural pain has not yet been studied.
2. Opioid analgesia: morphine or fentanyl are the most commonly
used opioids in the neonatal population. Opioids can
be administered either intravenously or via non-IV routes
(orally) for the treatment of acute pain. It can be given
continuously or as a single dose before the procedure (Bhalla
2014; Kinoshita 2023). There are still substantial gaps in
the knowledge surrounding sedation (e.g. midazolam) and
analgesia (e.g. opioids, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs,
acetaminophen) during mechanical ventilation in neonates; and
concerns remain about their safety, eficacy and short- and long-
term outcomes in mechanically ventilated neonates (Aranda
2005).
a. Morphine: alleviates prolonged pain, reduces behavioural
and hormonal stress responses and improves ventilator
synchrony and sedation. However, despite its routine use
in the NICU, morphine given as a loading dose followed
by continuous intravenous infusions does not provide
adequate analgesia for the acute pain caused by invasive
procedures amongst ventilated neonates (Carbajal 2005).
There are also concerns about adverse short- and long-
term neurodevelopmental outcomes related to the use of
morphine infusions in preterm neonates (AAP 2016). Some
side efects have been reported, such as hypotension,
constipation, urinary retention, respiratory depression,
duration of mechanical ventilation and development of
dependence and tolerance (Walker 2014).
b. Diamorphine works more quickly than morphine, reduces
the amount of histamine released and therefore causes
fewer hypotensive efects than morphine (Wood CM 1998).
Diamorphine was found to be efective in reducing stress
response (reduction of plasma cortisol and catecholamines)
in ventilated newborn neonates; adverse events described
were reduction of blood pressure, and, when diamorphine
was used in high doses (200 mcg/kg dosage), retention of
carbon dioxide along with a decrease in actual partial oxygen
pressure (Barker 1995).
c. Fentanyl: this drug is considered as a selective m-receptor
agonist and is almost one hundred times more potent than
morphine. It has a rapid, predictable onset of action with a
short duration of action, mostly due to its high lipid solubility.
Fentanyl gives greater haemodynamic stability. Although
fentanyl may be associated with rapid development of
tolerance and chest wall rigidity, it is the preferred analgesic
agent for critically ill patients. Fentanyl has been shown
to prevent neonates from surgical stress responses and to
improve postoperative outcomes (Maitra 2014; Walker 2014).
d. Remifentanil: a novel opioid. It was found to be at
least as efective as morphine-midazolam for endotracheal
intubation (Avino 2014). It gives intense analgesia and
anaesthesia, with a rapid recovery in various clinical
scenarios (Kamata 2016). It is not dependent on hepatic
metabolism and is eliminated by non-specific esterases.
The duration of action is not afected by the duration
of infusion. It makes rapid awakening possible. Reported
adverse events include: chest wall rigidity and decreased
thoracic compliance associated with hypoventilation,
oxygen desaturation, hypercarbia, decreased tidal volume
causing profound hypoxaemia, bradycardia and eventual
asystole. Other adverse events that may occur are
laryngospasm, hyperalgesia and tolerance (Bhalla 2014;
Kamata 2016).
e. Alfentanil: is a synthetic opioid chemically related to fentanyl.
It has a rapid onset and brief duration of action. It is used
as a procedural analgesic for paediatric patients. Reported
adverse events include muscle rigidity (Saarenmaa 1996).
f. Meperidine: Meperidine is a synthetic opiate agonist. It seems
to reduce sufering in mechanically ventilated neonates
and the duration of hypoxaemia associated with routine
treatment procedures (Pokela 1994). The use of meperidine
in neonates has not been thoroughly studied.

nervous system.

Why it is important to do this review
Review articles have reported the role of pharmacological
interventions during procedural pain in neonates (Carbajal
2005; Cignacco 2007; Ohlsson 2020). These interventions are
efective for many diferent acute procedures, but they may not
address procedures that are frequently repeated, such as ETS.
The role of pharmacological interventions during endotracheal
suctioning in ventilated neonates has not yet been appraised.
Endotracheal suctioning is ofen administered by a nurse
or a respiratory therapist (Gardner 2009). Although there is
an increase in adherence to national or international pain
guidelines, infant pain remains undertreated. Reducing painful
stimuli and interventions, and identifying efective pain-reducing
pharmacological interventions, is an obligation of researchers and
healthcare providers in the NICU. By performing this review, we
hope to ascertain which types of pharmacological interventions are
efective in pain management during endotracheal suctioning in
mechanically ventilated neonates.

To evaluate the benefits and harms of pharmacological

Criteria for considering studies for this review
Types of studies
We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs,
cluster-RCTs, and cross-over RCTs. We defined quasi-RCTs as those
where participants were allocated to diferent arms of the trial
using a method of allocation that is not truly random, such as date
of birth, medical record number, or date of recruitment.
Types of participants
Neonates include term and preterm infants.
We included:
1. neonates who were mechanically ventilated via endotracheal
tube and required endotracheal suctioning conducted by
doctors, nurses, physical therapists or other healthcare
professionals during their stay in the NICU;
2. neonates who had a tracheostomy and required suctioning
conducted by doctors, nurses, physical therapists or other
healthcare professionals during their stay in the NICU.
We classified term neonates as those whose post-menstrual age
(PMA) was from 37 completed weeks to a maximum of 44 weeks.
We classified preterm neonates using the World Health
Organization (WHO) criteria (WHO 2022).
1. Extremely preterm (less than 28 weeks' gestation).
2. Very preterm (from 28 up to 31 completed weeks' gestation).
3. Moderate-to-late preterm (from 32 to 36 completed weeks'
gestation).

We included pharmacological interventions applied during the
procedure of endotracheal suctioning, with the specific aim of
reducing pain or stress caused by the suctioning procedure. We

Types of outcome measures
Primary outcomes
Pain and discomfort were measured using at least one of the
following methods during the procedure (Hadian 2013).
1. Validated composite pain scores (including a combination of
behavioural, physiological and contextual indicators). Those
assessed in one Cochrane review as being valid for neonates
undergoing procedural pain included the following (Stevens
2016).
a. Premature Infant Pain Profile (PIPP): continuous scale,
ranging from 0 to 21; the higher the score, the more pain.
Included items are heart rate, oxygen saturation (SaO2),
tightly closing the eyes, changes in nose-lip and chin shape,
bulging of the brow between the eyes, gestational age, mode
of behaviour for pain assessment (Stevens 1996).
b. PIPP-revised (PIPP-R): revision of the PIPP to address validity
and feasibility issues; the minor revisions include changes
to the physical layout, detailed instructions for use, and
clarification of scoring gestational age and behavioural state
indicators for preterm and term neonates (Stevens 2014).
c. Douleur Aiguë du Nouveau-né Scale (DAN): continuous scale,
ranging from 0 to 10; the higher the score, the more pain.
Included items are facial responses, limb movements and
vocal expressions of pain (Carbajal 1997).
d. Neonatal Infant Pain Scale (NIPS): continuous scale, ranging
from 0 to 10. The higher the score, the more pain. Included
items are facial responses, limb movements and vocal
expressions of pain (Lawrence 1993).
e. Neonatal Facial Coding System (NFCS): an anatomically
based measure in which the occurrences of 10 diferent facial
actions are individually coded, ranging from 0 (minimum
pain) to 10 (maximum pain) (Grunau 1987).
f. Neurobehavioral Assessment of Preterm Infants (NAPI):
is a standardised neurodevelopmental assessment of the
progression of early neurobehavioural performance in
preterm neonates from 32 weeks to term age of 38 to 40
weeks, including the following seven clusters: scarf sign
(assessment of the tone of the shoulder girdle), motor
development and vigour, popliteals angle, alertness and
orientation, irritability, quality of cry and per cent sleep
ratings. Measurements in each cluster range from 0 to 100
points (Snider 2005).
g. Neonatal Pain Agitation and Sedation Scale (N-PASS):
continuous scale, ranging from −10 (deep sedation) to
+10 (highest level of pain); items included are crying and
irritability, behaviour state, facial expression, extremities and
tone, and vital signs (Hummel 2010).
h. Bernese Pain Scale for Neonates (BPSN): a multidimensional
pain assessment tool; included items are sleeping,
crying, consolation, skin colour, facial expression, posture,
breathing, heart rate and SaO2 (Cignacco 2004).
i. The Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario Pain Scale
(CHEOPS): continuous scale, ranging from 0 to 8. The
higher the score, the more pain. Included items are facial
expressions, cries, limbs and torso, movements, breathing
patterns (Saarenmaa 1996).

recovery following endotracheal suctioning.

we would have screened the list of included studies (Stevens 2000).
We contacted study authors for additional or missing information.
We excluded editorials, commentaries, reviews, lecture abstracts
and letters to the editor because they did not contain original data.
We searched for errata or retractions of included studies
using PubMed (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed) and the Retraction
Watch Database (https://retractiondatabase.org/).
Data collection and analysis
We used the standard methods of Cochrane and Cochrane
Neonatal.
Selection of studies
We managed search results using Endnote (EndNote). Results of the
search were screened using Covidence. We used the RCT Classifier
in Covidence to identify non-RCT records, and three review authors
(SP, FC and KB) independently screened the remaining title/
abstracts. The same authors independently reviewed the full texts
of studies retained following title/abstract review. At any point in
the screening process, disagreements were resolved by discussion.
We collated multiple reports of the same study, so that each study
rather than each report was the unit of interest in the review.
We recorded the selection process in suficient detail to complete a
PRISMA flow diagram (Page 2021a; Page 2021b), and Characteristics
of excluded studies table.
Data extraction and management
Two review authors (SP, IO) independently extracted data from the
full-text articles using a specifically designed spreadsheet including
the following details.
1. Authors;
2. Date and place of publication;
3. Study design: methods of randomisation, number of arms in the
trial, cross-over design, single- or multicentre;
4. Inclusion and exclusion criteria;
5. Number of participants in each arm (including dropouts);
6. Setting;
7. Summary of study participant characteristics: gestational age
and weight at birth, postmenstrual and postnatal age at time of
enrolment, sex;
8. Details of intervention (type of intervention, description of non-
pharmacological actions, duration of intervention) and control;
9. Adverse events;
10.Outcome measurements and assessment time points;
11.Risk of bias;
12.Any relevant additional comments reported by the study
authors.
We compared extracted data for any diferences. We resolved
diferences through discussion. If necessary, we consulted a third
review author (FC) to reach consensus.
Assessment of risk of bias in included studies
Two review authors (SP, FC) independently assessed the risk of bias
(low, high, or unclear) of all included trials using the Cochrane RoB
1 tool (Higgins 2011); for the following domains.
1. Sequence generation (selection bias);
2. Allocation concealment (selection bias);
3. Blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias);
4. Blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias);
5. Incomplete outcome data (attrition bias);
6. Selective reporting (reporting bias);
7. Any other bias.
We resolved any disagreements by discussion or by consulting with
a third review author (FC). See Appendix 2 for a more detailed
description of the risk of bias for each domain.
Measures of treatment efect
We used RevMan 2024 to analyse treatment efects in the individual
trials.
Continuous data
We reported continuous data as mean diference (MD) with a 95%
confidence interval (CI).
Dichotomous data
We reported dichotomous data using a risk ratio (RR) and risk
diference (RD), with respective 95% CIs. For those outcomes with
a statistically significant RD for the pooled estimate from the
meta-analysis, we calculated the number needed to treat for an
additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) or the number needed to
treat for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH), and 95% CIs.
Unit of analysis issues
For parallel-group studies with individual randomisation, the unit
of analysis was the individual participant.
Data from cluster-RCTs, where groups of participants were
randomised instead of individuals, were only included in a meta-
analysis if a measure of efect (e.g. odds ratio (OR) with 95% CI) was
available from an analysis which accounted properly for clustering
(Higgins 2022).
If meta-analysis of cross-over trials had been performed, we would
have based meta-analyses only on data from the first allocation
period (if those data were available) (Higgins 2022), and only for
the very short-term treatment efects (i.e. measured during and
immediately afer the suctioning procedure). We did not include
treatment efects measured during allocation periods afer cross-
over, and longer-term treatment efects were not included in the
analyses because of the risk 'carry-over' efects (Higgins 2022).
No meta-analyses of cross-over trials were performed.

Dealing with missing data
We contacted the study authors to request missing data. In the
case of missing data, we presented the number of participants
with the missing data in the results section and the Characteristics
of included studies table. We presented only the results of the
available participants. We discussed the implications of the missing
data in the Discussion.
Assessment of heterogeneity
We used the formal statistics described below.
1. The Chi2 test for homogeneity (P value less than 0.1) to calculate
whether statistical heterogeneity was present. Since this test has
low power when the number of studies included in the meta-
analysis was small, the probability was set at the 10% level of
significance.
2. The impact of statistical heterogeneity using the I2 statistic,
available in Review Manager (RevMan 2024), which describes the
percentage of total variation across studies due to heterogeneity
rather than sampling error. This value is interpreted based on the
following thresholds, as identified in the Cochrane Handbook for
Systematic Reviews of Interventions (Higgins 2022):
a. less than 25% as no heterogeneity;
b. 25% to 49% as low heterogeneity;
c. 50% to 74% as moderate heterogeneity; and
d. 75% and above as high heterogeneity.
Where there was evidence of apparent or statistical heterogeneity,
we assessed the source of the heterogeneity - such as between trial
diferences in the population or diferences in the delivery of the
intervention, using sensitivity and subgroup analyses looking for
evidence of bias or methodological diferences between trials.
Assessment of reporting biases
We planned to investigate reporting and publication bias by
examining the degree of asymmetry of a funnel plot if the number of
trials included in the meta-analysis was 10 or more. We were unable
to do so because we included only seven RCTs (10 references) in our
review.
Where bias was suspected, we attempted to contact the study
authors to ask them to provide missing outcome data. Where this
was not possible, and the missing data were thought to introduce
serious bias, we explored the impact of including such studies in the
overall assessment of results using a sensitivity analysis.
Data synthesis
We used the statistical package Review Manager to perform meta-
analysis (RevMan 2024). For categorical outcomes, we calculated
the typical estimates of RR and RD, each with its 95% CI; for
continuous outcomes, we calculated the MD or SMD, each with its
95% CI. We used a fixed-efect model to combine data where it
was reasonable to assume that studies were estimating the same
underlying treatment efect. If there was evidence of high statistical
heterogeneity (I2 statistic 75% or greater), we planned to evaluate
this based on the diferent study characteristics and subgroup
analysis. We planned to use the generic inverse variance method.
Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity
We planned to conduct the following subgroup analyses for the
primary outcome, if the information was available, by examining
the overlap of the CIs of the summary efect estimates for the
subgroups, and by performing a Chi2 test for homogeneity and
calculating an I2 value for between-subgroup diferences.
1. Term versus preterm neonates (see Types of participants for
definitions);
2. Endotracheal intubation versus tracheostomy.
We were unable to perform subgroup analyses; most of the
trials were only of preterm babies and there were no trials with
tracheostomy.
Sensitivity analysis
We performed sensitivity analyses to explore the impact of:
1. The choice of statistical model (fixed-efect versus random-
efects);
2. Methodological quality, by excluding studies with a high risk of
bias;
3. Missing data; we presented only the results of the available
participants.
The main conclusions remained consistent afer sensitivity
analysis.
Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the
evidence
We used the GRADE approach, as outlined in the GRADE Handbook
(Schünemann 2013). The following outcomes were assessed in the
Summary of Findings tables:
1. Validated composite pain scores
a. PIPP
b. CHEOPS change from baseline
2. Physiological indicators
a. Heart rate change
3. Behavioural indicators

4. Pulmonary outcomes
a. Duration of mechanical ventilation
5. Haemodynamic changes
6. Neurological outcome

considered evidence from RCTs as high-certainty, but downgraded

Results of the search
Searches identified 3461 references; afer removing 1193
duplicates; 2268 were available for screening. We excluded 2248
references based on title abstract (173 via the Covidence automatic
classifier system and 2075 by authors). We reviewed 20 full texts and
included seven studies (10 references) and excluded nine studies
(10 references). We identified no ongoing trials. Details of the
selection process are available in Figure 1.
Two authors were contacted twice to obtain detailed results
in January 2020 (Anand 2008; Pokela 1994). No response was
received.
The characteristics of studies are summarised below; further
detail is provided in the Characteristics of included studies and
Characteristics of excluded studies.
Included studies
We included seven trials (10 reports) that enroled 1242 neonates.
Full details of the seven included studies are given in the
Characteristics of included studies table.
Participants
Six of the seven studies enroled preterm neonates (Anand 1999;
Anand 2008; Cignacco 2008; Saarenmaa 1996; Saarenmaa 2001;
Simons 2013).
One study included both preterm and term neonates (Pokela 1994).
Interventions
Four studies examined the efect of morphine administration on
pain during endotracheal suctioning, either as continuous infusion
during the period of mechanical ventilation (Anand 1999; Anand
2008; Simons 2013), or as intermittent boluses prior to suctioning
(Cignacco 2008).
One study examined the use of midazolam continuous infusion
(Anand 1999), and another study alfentanil boluses (Saarenmaa
1996). Other interventions studied were: ketamine boluses
(Saarenmaa 2001), and meperidine boluses (Pokela 1994).
Outcome measures
Outcome measures varied amongst studies, ofen including more
than one outcome.
The Premature Infant Pain Profile (PIPP) was used in four studies
(Anand 1999; Anand 2008; Cignacco 2008; Simons 2013), whereas
the Neonatal Infant Pain Scale (NIPS) was used in only one study
(Simons 2013). One study used the visual analogue scale (VAS)
(Simons 2013). The Bernese Pain Scale for Neonates (BPSN) was
used in one study (Cignacco 2008), and the Children's Hospital
of Eastern Ontario Pain Scale (CHEOPS) was used in two studies
(Saarenmaa 1996; Saarenmaa 2001). One study used COMFORT
scores (Simons 2013). A behavioural pain score was used in one
study (Pokela 1994).

Random sequence
Five studies described the method of randomisation: based
on a computer list; computer random-number generator;
automated telephone response system and numbers taken from
a randomisation table (low risk of bias; Anand 1999; Anand 2008;
Cignacco 2008; Pokela 1994; Simons 2013). We judged two studies
to have unclear risk of bias. Two studies did not provide an
adequate description of the methods used (Saarenmaa 1996,
Saarenmaa 2001).
Allocation concealment
Allocation concealment was adequate in six studies (low risk
of bias; Anand 1999; Anand 2008; Cignacco 2008; Saarenmaa
1996; Saarenmaa 2001; Simons 2013). In one study, insuficient
information was supplied to adequately assess allocation
concealment (unclear risk of bias: Pokela 1994).
Blinding
Blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias) (all
outcomes)
Blinding to avoid performance bias was adequate in all seven
studies (Anand 1999; Anand 2008; Cignacco 2008; Pokela 1994;
Saarenmaa 1996; Saarenmaa 2001; Simons 2013).
Blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias) (all outcomes)
Blinding to avoid detection bias was adequate in all seven studies
(Anand 1999; Anand 2008; Cignacco 2008; Pokela 1994; Saarenmaa
1996; Saarenmaa 2001; Simons 2013).
Incomplete outcome data
Four studies had complete outcome data (low risk of bias; Anand
2008; Cignacco 2008; Saarenmaa 1996; Simons 2013). Three studies
provided no information on the number of neonates analysed, and
a patient flow diagram was not available (unclear risk of bias; Anand
1999; Pokela 1994; Saarenmaa 2001).
Selective reporting
We tried to get access to the protocol of the included studies
by contacting the study authors. The protocol was available and
reporting was adequate in three studies (low risk of bias; Anand
1999; Anand 2008; Cignacco 2008).
Reporting was unclear in three studies (unclear risk of bias;
Saarenmaa 1996; Saarenmaa 2001; Simons 2013).
In one study, there was no power calculation and no primary
hypothesis (high risk of bias; Pokela 1994).
Other potential sources of bias
Five studies had no other source of possible bias (low risk of bias;
Anand 1999; Anand 2008; Simons 2013). Two studies had cross-over
designs which could cause a carry-over efect (high risk of bias;
Saarenmaa 1996; Saarenmaa 2001).

D I S C U S S I O N
Summary of main results
The results are summarised in Summary of findings 1; Summary of
findings 2; and Summary of findings 3.
Seven trials, including 1242 neonates, investigated the efects
of pharmacological interventions for the prevention of pain
during endotracheal suctioning. The interventions were morphine,
alfentanil, meperidine, midazolam and ketamine. The efect on
pain was assessed using validated pain assessment scales such
as PIPP, CHEOPS, BPSN, VAS, NIPS, and COMFORT; physiological
indicator changes from baseline, such as heart rate; or behavioural
indicators such as BPS.
Four studies were combined in a meta-analysis (Anand 1999; Anand
2008; Cignacco 2008; Simons 2013). The largest study included in
any analysis was Anand 2008, which reported on 898 neonates. The
meta-analysis with the largest number of participants was for the
PIPP scale, 1123 neonates (4 studies).
Opioids, administered as continuous infusion or as boluses
prior to suctioning compared to placebo during endotracheal
suctioning:
Morphine may have little to no efect on PIPP scores and on
the duration of mechanical ventilation, but the evidence is
very uncertain. Morphine may not increase the risk of arterial
hypotension and probably does not reduce the incidence of severe
IVH.
Alfentanil 20 µg/kg may reduce CHEOPS change and heart rate
change from baseline, but the evidence is very uncertain.
Meperidine may reduce BPS.
Opioids compared to sedatives during endotracheal suctioning:
Morphine may have little to no efect on PIPP scores, compared to
midazolam, but the evidence is very uncertain.
Morphine may result in a large reduction in duration of mechanical
ventilation, compared to midazolam.
No studies reported on physiological and behavioural indicators or
haemodynamic changes.
Morphine may not reduce the incidence of severe IVH, compared to
midazolam.
Sedatives compared to placebo during endotracheal suctioning:
Midazolam may reduce PIPP scores.
Ketamine 1 mg/kg may reduce CHEOPS change from baseline, but
the evidence is very uncertain.
Ketamine 0.5 mg/kg and 2 mg/kg may have little to no efect on
CHEOPS change from baseline, but the evidence is very uncertain.

Overall completeness and applicability of evidence
Prevention of pain during endotracheal suctioning through the
use of pharmacological interventions has only been studied
in seven trials that included 1255 neonates. Due to the high
heterogeneity in the interventions studied, only four studies
could be combined in a meta-analysis. Morphine is the only
pharmacological intervention with a large study population (1123
neonates), albeit predominantly as a continuous infusion for the
prevention of pain during mechanical ventilation, rather than an
intervention focusing on pain specifically caused by endotracheal
suctioning.
Six out of seven studies reported only on preterm neonates (Anand
1999; Anand 2008; Cignacco 2008; Saarenmaa 1996; Saarenmaa
2001; Simons 2013); only one study reported on both term and
preterm neonates (Pokela 1994).
No studies reported the following comparisons: non-opioid
analgesia versus placebo or other drugs with analgesic/sedative
efect acting on the central nervous system or opioid analgesia;
opioids versus non-pharmacological interventions; and other
drugs with analgesic/sedative efect acting on the central nervous
system versus non-pharmacological interventions. Information on
the efects of other opioids or sedative drugs is very limited. Newer
drugs such as propofol or dexmedetomidine have not been studied
at all. Due to the large variation in interventions on the one hand,
and missing information about the prespecified outcomes, on the
other hand, the statistical combination of study results in a meta-
analysis was limited.
Four out of the seven studies were performed more than 20 years
ago. As a result, the extremely low gestational age infant is poorly
represented in the study populations. Nowadays, mechanical
ventilation is largely performed in the fragile subgroup of preterm
neonates, in which the use of analgesic and sedative drugs may be
associated with long-term efects.
Quality of the evidence
The certainty of evidence is summarised in Summary of findings 1;
Summary of findings 2; and Summary of findings 3, and varied from
very low to moderate.
While there is very low-to-moderate evidence for opioids, the
certainty of evidence is very low to low for sedatives. The GRADE
assessments rely heavily on the risk of bias in the trials, and
the inconsistency and imprecision of their results, mainly due to
small sample sizes. The very low certainty of evidence for opioids
stems from serious inconsistency and imprecision. Although the
efect of morphine was investigated in a larger study population,
the interventions studied were heterogeneous with regard to
mode of administration (continuous infusion in three studies
versus intermittent boluses in one study) and dose (30 µg/kg/
h versus 10 µg/kg/h). This could explain the high degree of
statistical heterogeneity (I2 = 93%) in the meta-analysis for the main
comparison, morphine versus placebo. Only one study reported on
both preterm and term neonates, and only one study prespecified
subgroups based on gestational age at study entry (24 to 26 weeks,
27 to 29 weeks and 30 to 33 weeks) in order to administer age-
appropriate doses of the analgesic, and also reported primary
outcomes by subgroup (Anand 2008). It is well known that both the
pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of drugs administered
to neonates are strongly dependent on organ maturity. The low
certainty of evidence for sedatives stems from the high risk of bias
and serious imprecision due to very few events, with sizes varying
between 10 and 84 neonates, resulting in serious imprecision of
efect estimates and risk of random error. Two of the trials had a
cross-over design introducing a substantial risk of carry-over efects
(Saarenmaa 1996; Saarenmaa 2001).
Although all studies used validated pain assessment instruments,
measurement of pain in premature neonates, especially the most
immature ones, remains challenging and somewhat subjective and
observer-dependent. Assessment tools should be further improved
in order to accurately reflect the level of pain or discomfort in this
specific patient population.
Most trials focused on pain during the suctioning procedure. The
length of observation and return to baseline was not taken into
account.
Preventing and reducing pain or stress in neonates starts with
adaptations of procedural techniques or practices. Strategies such
as reducing light and noise, facilitated tucking or swaddling,
minimising patient handling and tailored nursing techniques could
be very powerful in the prevention of pain (Alinejad-Naeini 2014;
Allegaert 2013; Axelin 2006; Cone 2013; Lago 2009; Ward-Larson
2004). None of the included studies indicated that environmental
factors such as light and noise were taken into account when
performing the intervention. The way the endotracheal suctioning
was performed and by whom it was done, also difered between
the studies. In one study, daily routine procedures were performed
at the same time as endotracheal suctioning (Pokela 1994), most
likely afecting the pain scores measured during the procedure.
In two studies, the infant was manually ventilated during the
intervention (Saarenmaa 1996; Saarenmaa 2001). Pre-oxygenation,
by increasing the inspired fraction of oxygen by 10% prior to
endotracheal suctioning, was only described in one study (Pokela
1994). Mostly, details of the suctioning procedure, such as the
volume of instillation or the insertion depth of the suction probe,
were lacking, while these factors may considerably influence pain
and stress during endotracheal suctioning.
Three studies mentioned endotracheal suctioning being performed
by qualified and trained nurses (Cignacco 2008; Pokela 1994;
Simons 2013). In the other studies, it was not specified by whom the
intervention was performed or whether the observer was qualified
to measure pain. Previous research has shown that theoretical and
practical education of nurses, the implementation of guidelines
on endotracheal suctioning and training in the assessment of

Potential biases in the review process
To prevent potential biases in the review, we conducted
extensive searches of the published and unpublished literature on
pharmacological interventions for the prevention of pain during
endotracheal suctioning in ventilated neonates. Three review
authors (SP, FC and KB) selected the trials from the literature
searches, completed predesigned forms for data abstraction (SP,
IO), and performed risk of bias assessment (SP, FC). We discussed
any discrepancies and resolved them by consensus. The final
decision remains a clinical judgement.
This review was limited by the few studies that were identified,
the low number of participants, and the moderate-to-very-low-
certainty of the available evidence.
There might also be a diference in the prevention of
pain during endotracheal suctioning between continuous
opioid administration and bolus administration. There was no
study comparing continuous opioid administration with bolus
administration.
The review methods did not allow detection of serious or rare
adverse events.
Agreements and disagreements with other studies or
reviews
This systematic review with meta-analysis is the first to evaluate
pharmacological pain-reducing interventions during endotracheal
suctioning. The use of morphine and midazolam for the prevention
of pain has already been thoroughly described in other reviews
regarding procedural pain (Bellù 2008; Taddio 2017).
Of all opioids, morphine is the most administered analgesic in
neonates. Despite its widespread use for neonatal pain, it does
not seem to provide adequate analgesia for acute pain caused
by invasive procedures amongst ventilated neonates (Bellù 2008;
Carbajal 2005), which is also confirmed in this review.
Besides morphine, fentanyl and its derivatives are also commonly
used in neonates. Although its eficacy and haemodynamic safety
in children has been well proven, serious adverse events (chest
wall rigidity and respiratory depression), especially in preterm and
term neonates, have been reported in this review as well as in
previous research (Choong 2010; Pereira 2007). Alfentanil is one
of its derivatives and, although there has been some research,
suficient evidence lacks to recommend its use in newborn
neonates (Ziesenitz 2018). Another derivative of fentanyl that has
recently been studied is remifentanil. Due to its rapid onset of
action and clearance, it seems promising for procedural pain during
short procedures, such as endotracheal intubation.
The use of meperidine has not been thoroughly investigated in
neonates. Adverse events described in neonates and children are
orofacial dyskinesias, severe muscle rigidity and seizures (Baris
2000; Kyf 1990; Saneto 1996). As other, safer opioids are available,
there is a recommendation against the use of meperidine for the
management of pain in neonates (AAP 2001; Thigpen 2019).
The use of ketamine for procedural pain in neonates has also been
poorly investigated. One study investigating the use of ketamine
in combination with atropine during a less invasive surfactant
administration (LISA) procedure resulted in low pain scores and
haemodynamic stability, but also in prolonged desaturations and
apnoea, necessitating intubation (Bourgoin 2018).
According to a Cochrane review, there is insuficient evidence to
promote the use of midazolam in ventilated neonates. Although it
efectively reduces pain in neonates compared to placebo, there
are some safety concerns associated with the use of midazolam
(Taddio 2017).

Implications for practice
In mechanically ventilated newborn neonates, morphine may have
little to no efect on PIPP or duration of ventilation (evidence is very
uncertain). Morphine may not increase the risk of hypotension and
probably does not reduce the incidence of severe IVH. Alfentanil
may reduce CHEOPS and heart rate change from baseline (evidence
is very uncertain). Meperidine may reduce BPS.
Compared to midazolam, morphine may have little to no efect
on PIPP scores, and may result in a large reduction in duration
of ventilation (evidence is very uncertain). No studies reported
on physiological and behavioural indicators or haemodynamic
changes. Morphine may not reduce the incidence of severe IVH,
compared to midazolam (low-certainty evidence).
Compared to placebo, midazolam may reduce PIPP scores; has
little to no efect on the duration of ventilation or on the risk of
severe IVH, (low to very low-certainty evidence); and ketamine
may reduce CHEOPS change, have little to no efect on heart
rate change, or on mean arterial blood pressure (evidence very-
uncertain). No studies reported on behavioural outcomes.
Implications for research
When using analgo-sedative drugs in newborn neonates in
a neonatal intensive care unit, the balance between the
neuroprotective efect of pain prevention and the potential
neurotoxicity of the drug itself on brain development is delicate.
The ultimate goal should be to optimise brain growth and improve
outcomes.
Based on the results of this review, there are gaps in the existing
literature on the prevention of pain during endotracheal suctioning.
Future research should focus on the following:
1. Improved tailoring of both pharmacological and non-
pharmacological interventions to reduce pain in neonates.
2. The diference in pain perception and pain management
between preterm and term neonates.

Appendix 2. Risk of bias 1 (RoB 1) tool
We used the standard methods of Cochrane and Cochrane Neonatal to assess the methodological quality of the trials. For each trial, we
planned to seek information regarding the method of randomisation, blinding and reporting of all outcomes of all the infants enroled in
the trial. We assessed each criterion as being at a low, high, or unclear risk of bias. Two review authors separately assessed each study.
We resolved any disagreement by discussion. We added this information to the Characteristics of included studies table. We evaluated the
following issues and entered the findings into the risk of bias table.
1. Sequence generation (checking for possible selection bias). Was the allocation sequence adequately generated?
For each included study, we categorised the method used to generate the allocation sequence as:
1. low risk (any truly random process, e.g. random number table; computer random number generator);
2. high risk (any non-random process, e.g. odd or even date of birth; hospital or clinic record number); or
3. unclear risk.
2. Allocation concealment (checking for possible selection bias). Was allocation adequately concealed?
For each included study, we categorised the method used to conceal the allocation sequence as:
1. low risk (e.g. telephone or central randomisation; consecutively numbered sealed opaque envelopes);
2. high risk (open random allocation; unsealed or non-opaque envelopes, alternation; date of birth); or
3. unclear risk.
3. Blinding of participants and personnel (checking for possible performance bias). Was knowledge of the allocated intervention
adequately prevented during the study?
For each included study, we categorised the methods used to blind study participants and personnel from knowledge of which intervention
a participant received. Blinding was assessed separately for diferent outcomes or class of outcomes. We categorised the methods as:
1. low risk, high risk or unclear risk for participants; and
2. low risk, high risk or unclear risk for personnel.
4. Blinding of outcome assessment (checking for possible detection bias). Was knowledge of the allocated intervention
adequately prevented at the time of outcome assessment?
For each included study, we categorised the methods used to blind outcome assessment. Blinding was assessed separately for diferent
outcomes or class of outcomes. We categorised the methods as:
1. low risk for outcome assessors;
2. high risk for outcome assessors; or
3. unclear risk for outcome assessors.
5. Incomplete outcome data (checking for possible attrition bias through withdrawals, dropouts, protocol deviations). Were
incomplete outcome data adequately addressed?
For each included study and for each outcome, we described the completeness of data including attrition and exclusions from the analysis.
We noted whether attrition and exclusions were reported, the numbers included in the analysis at each stage (compared with the total
randomised participants), reasons for attrition or exclusion where reported, and whether missing data were balanced across groups or
were related to outcomes. Where suficient information is reported or supplied by the trial authors, we re-included missing data in the
analyses. We categorised the methods as:
1. low risk (less than 20% missing data);
2. high risk (20% or greater missing data); or
3. unclear risk.

6. Selective reporting bias. Are reports of the study free of suggestion of selective outcome reporting?
For each included study, we described how we investigated the possibility of selective outcome reporting bias and what we found. For
studies in which study protocols were published in advance, we compared prespecified outcomes versus outcomes eventually reported in
the published results. If the study protocol was not published in advance, we contacted study authors to gain access to the study protocol.
We assessed the methods as:
1. low risk (where it is clear that all the study's prespecified outcomes and all expected outcomes of interest to the review have been
reported);
2. high risk (where not all the study's prespecified outcomes have been reported; one or more reported primary outcomes were not
prespecified outcomes of interest and are reported incompletely and so cannot be used; study fails to include results of a key outcome
that would have been expected to have been reported); or
3. unclear risk.
7. Other sources of bias. Was the study apparently free of other problems that could put it at a high risk of bias?
For each included study, we described any important concerns we had about other possible sources of bias (for example, whether there
was a potential source of bias related to the specific study design or whether the trial was stopped early due to some data-dependent
process). We assessed whether each study was free of other problems that could put it at risk of bias as:
1. low risk;
2. high risk;
3. unclear risk.
If needed, we planned to explore the impact of the level of bias through undertaking sensitivity analyses.

pharmacological interventions applied during the procedure of endotracheal suctioning, with the specific aim of reducing pain or
stress caused by the suctioning procedure.
◦ We excluded studies about pain management for other procedures.
◦ We provided definitions of the study designs eligible for inclusion.
◦ We added a sentence to explicitly state that we excluded studies about pain management for other procedures; this aligns with the
published protocol.
◦ We added more examples of analgesics to clarify that we included studies of any analgesics; this aligns with the comparisons stated
in the published protocol: under opioid analgesia, alfentanil and meperidine were added.
◦ We reordered the comparisons and listed opioids first because opioids are the most commonly used intervention for suctioning, and
we believe the most used interventions will be of most interest to readers.
◦ We changed comparisons to a more granular level for clarity, e.g. the protocol stated “Non-opioid analgesia versus placebo,
no treatment, or non-pharmacological interventions.” The review states: 1. Opioids compared to placebo for pain during
endotracheal suctioning. 2. Opioids compared to non-pharmacological interventions. 3. Opioids compared to sedatives.
4. Sedatives compared to placebo. 5. Other drugs with analgesic/sedative efects acting on the central nervous system
compared to non-pharmacological interventions. 6. Non-opioid analgesia compared to placebo, no treatment, or non-
pharmacological interventions. 7. Non-opioid analgesia compared to opioid analgesia. 8. Non-opioid analgesia compared to
other drugs with analgesic/sedative efects acting on the central nervous system.
•
Outcome measures:
◦ We added the names of additional pain scales, CHEOPS, and BPS.
◦ In the protocol, behavioural indicators were listed within the pain outcome; in the review we listed behavioural outcomes in a
separate category.
◦ In the secondary pulmonary outcomes, pneumonia, hypoxaemia and chronic lung disease were added.
◦ We changed the timing of outcome measurement to during the procedure and did not measure five minutes before or 10 minutes
afer to more clearly align with the title and objective of the review.
•
We made the following edit to the 'Unit of analysis issues'. The protocol stated that short-term treatment efects would be measured
during and immediately afer the suctioning procedure. In the review, we stated that short- and long-term treatment efects would be
measured.
•
We initially planned to use a random-efects model to perform the meta-analysis, but to be in line with the guidelines of Cochrane
Neonatal, we used a fixed-efects model.
